title: SHOULD CHRISTIAN PARENTS CUT OFF AN ADULT CHILD WHO REJECTS THEIR FAITH? WHAT IF THE CHILD YOU RAISED TO LOVE JESUS NO LONGER WANTS HIM?
paragraphs: SHOULD CHRISTIAN PARENTS CUT OFF AN ADULT CHILD WHO REJECTS THEIR FAITH? WHAT IF THE CHILD YOU RAISED TO LOVE JESUS NO LONGER WANTS HIM?

When your child walks away from the faith, should you close the door to protect your convictions—or leave the light on because you remember the Savior who never stopped calling sinners home? The biblical answer may challenge both the parents who want to hold on and those who are ready to let go.
There is a particular kind of heartbreak that doesn't come with a funeral.
Your child is still alive.
Still breathing. Still posting pictures. Still laughing with friends. Still making plans for tomorrow.
But the little boy who once folded his hands beside his bed and whispered, "Dear Jesus, thank You for Mommy and Daddy," now says he doesn't believe in God.
The little girl who used to sing worship songs in the back seat of your car now tells you she wants nothing to do with Christianity.
And suddenly, the house that once echoed with bedtime prayers feels painfully quiet.
You remember dedicating that child to the Lord.
You remember the Sunday school lessons, the Bible stories, the prayers before examinations, the whispered blessings over a sleeping forehead.
You remember begging God to protect that child from the world.
But you never imagined that one day, the world would seem more believable to your child than the God you taught them to love.
Then comes the conversation you have been dreading.
"Mom, Dad... I don't believe what you believe anymore."
Perhaps they say Christianity is too restrictive.
Perhaps they have questions you cannot answer.
Perhaps they have been wounded by Christians.
Perhaps they have chosen a lifestyle that conflicts with your understanding of Scripture.
Or perhaps they simply look you in the eyes and say something that makes your stomach drop.
"Please stop trying to make me believe."
And now you are standing at a crossroads no parenting book prepared you for.
Do you keep calling?
Do you invite them home for Christmas?
Do you allow them around the younger children?
Do you tell them they are welcome at your table even when they openly reject the faith that built your home?
Or do you cut them off, hoping the pain of separation will finally bring them to repentance?
Before you answer, there is something you need to understand.
You can refuse to compromise the truth without refusing to love the person who rejects it.
And if that sentence makes you uncomfortable, stay with me.

Because Jesus told a story about a father, a rebellious son, a broken relationship, and a road that would eventually become the setting for one of the most extraordinary pictures of grace in all of Scripture.
But the detail that changes everything is not simply that the son came home.
It is what the father did when he saw him.
In Luke 15, Jesus tells us about a younger son who demanded his inheritance while his father was still alive.
In the cultural setting of the story, the demand was profoundly dishonoring. The son wanted the benefits of his father's estate without remaining under his father's household.
He wanted the gifts.
Not the relationship.
He wanted freedom.
Not responsibility.
He wanted the inheritance.
Not the father.
And the father let him go.
Read that again.
The father let him go.
He did not chain him to the house.
He did not manufacture a false confession.
He did not demand that the son pretend to love what he had already rejected.
The son left, squandered his wealth, and eventually found himself desperate and hungry.
Then Jesus gives us these remarkable words in Luke 15:17:
"And when he came to himself..."
The Greek expression is εἰς ἑαυτὸν δὲ ἐλθὼν (eis heauton de elthōn).
Literally, the phrase conveys the idea of coming to himself, or coming to his senses.
The son began to recognize the reality of his condition.
But notice something.
The father did not travel to the distant country to force his son into repentance.
He did not pretend the rebellion was harmless.
He did not finance the son's destructive living indefinitely.
Yet nothing in the story suggests that the father had stopped loving him.
And when the son finally returned, Scripture says:
"But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." — Luke 15:20, KJV
The Greek word translated "had compassion" is ἐσπλαγχνίσθη (esplanchnisthē), from a verb expressing deep, inward compassion.
This was not a father casually tolerating his son's return.
This was compassion that moved him to action.
He ran.
In a culture where the dignified behavior of an older household patriarch mattered, that image is striking.
The father moved toward the son who had dishonored him.
Not because rebellion had suddenly become righteousness.
Not because truth no longer mattered.
But because the lost son had returned.
And here is where many Christian parents need to hear something difficult.
The father did not have to approve of the distant country to welcome his son home.
But we must also read the parable carefully.

The son in Luke 15 returned acknowledging his sin. Jesus was describing the joy of repentance and restoration, not giving a blanket command that parents must accept every behavior or remove every boundary.
The father represents God's gracious welcome of the repentant sinner. He is not a complete instruction manual for every difficult family situation.
Still, the story reveals something precious about the heart of God.
His mercy is not reluctant.
His compassion is not cold.
And His grace does not require Him to call evil good.
So what does that mean when your adult child rejects Christianity?
It means you must learn the difference between loving your child and affirming everything your child believes.
Those are not the same thing.
You can say, "I believe Jesus Christ is the only way to the Father," because Jesus Himself said so in John 14:6.
You can say, "I cannot call something righteous when Scripture calls it sin."
You can refuse to participate in actions that violate your conscience.
You can remain faithful to the Gospel without rewriting biblical teaching to avoid an uncomfortable conversation.
But you can also say:
"You are still my child."
"I still love you."
"You are welcome to speak honestly with me."
"I will not pretend we agree, but I will not treat you as worthless because we disagree."
And perhaps the most difficult sentence of all:
"I cannot make you believe. But I will continue praying for you."
Some parents are afraid that this kind of love will communicate approval.
But the Bible never teaches that kindness automatically equals compromise.
Romans 2:4 speaks of the kindness of God leading toward repentance.
The Greek word χρηστότης (chrēstotēs) refers to kindness or goodness.
God's kindness does not erase His holiness.
It reveals His patience toward sinners.
And if God's kindness can serve His purpose of leading people toward repentance, why should Christian parents assume that cruelty is a better instrument of spiritual restoration?
Think about that.
When did humiliation become a fruit of the Spirit?
When did emotional punishment become a substitute for discipleship?
When did refusing to answer your child's phone calls become proof of biblical courage?
Galatians 5:22–23 identifies the fruit of the Spirit as love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, and temperance.
It does not list manipulation.
It does not list contempt.
It does not list using affection as a weapon.
And yet some Christian parents, out of genuine fear for their children's souls, begin doing exactly that.
They turn every dinner into a debate.
Every phone call into a sermon.
Every family gathering into an interrogation.
They begin treating their adult child's spiritual condition as a problem that must be solved before a relationship can exist.
And slowly, the child stops visiting.
Stops calling.
Stops sharing.
Not necessarily because the child has stopped loving the parents.
Sometimes because every interaction has become another opportunity to feel condemned, cornered, or unheard.
Now, this does not mean every accusation of judgment is fair. Faithful biblical correction can be painful, and people sometimes reject truth precisely because it challenges them.
But Christian parents must be willing to examine their own conduct.
Because there is a difference between someone being offended by the Gospel and someone being wounded by our pride.
Do not confuse your child's rejection of Christ with your child's rejection of the way you have represented Christ.
Those two things may overlap.
But they are not always identical.
And this is where the story becomes even more uncomfortable.
What if your child did not walk away from Christianity because they never heard the Gospel?
What if they heard plenty of religious language but rarely experienced confession, humility, or forgiveness at home?
What if they watched you worship on Sunday and tear people apart on Monday?
What if they saw you quote Scripture to correct them but never heard you use Scripture to correct yourself?
What if they learned that admitting doubt brought punishment rather than patient conversation?
What if the wounds they associate with Christianity came from the very people who were supposed to demonstrate Christlike love?
That possibility does not excuse unbelief.
Parents are not responsible for every decision an adult child makes.
And even faithful, loving parents can have children who reject the faith.
But if we want our children to take repentance seriously, we must be willing to practice it ourselves.
Imagine the power of a father looking his adult son in the eyes and saying:
"I still believe the Bible is true. But I also realize that I have sometimes used my anger in ways that dishonored the Lord. I was wrong. Will you forgive me?"
Imagine a mother saying:
"I cannot change what Scripture teaches. But I can change how I speak to you. I want to listen better."
That is not surrendering biblical authority.
That is submitting to it.
Because the same Bible that commands children to honor their parents also warns fathers not to provoke their children to wrath (Ephesians 6:4).
The same Scriptures that call believers to speak the truth also command them to speak it in love (Ephesians 4:15).
And James 1:19 calls us to be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to wrath.
Sometimes the most powerful Gospel conversation begins when a parent stops preparing a rebuttal long enough to hear the pain behind the question.
But perhaps you are thinking:
"Doesn't the Bible command Christians to separate from unbelievers?"
That question deserves an honest answer.
Scripture does command believers to reject idolatry, refuse participation in sin, and exercise appropriate church discipline.

Second Corinthians 6:14 warns believers against being unequally yoked with unbelievers. Its surrounding context concerns partnerships that compromise loyalty to God, not a universal prohibition against maintaining family relationships with nonbelievers.
First Corinthians 5 discusses church discipline for a person who claims to belong to the Christian community while persisting in serious, unrepentant sin.
But Paul makes an important distinction in verses 9–13.
He explains that his instruction is not a command to avoid all immoral people outside the church.
Otherwise, believers would have to leave the world altogether.
The church has a responsibility to address serious sin among those who profess membership in the believing community.
That is not the same as ordering Christian parents to abandon an adult child simply because that child does not profess faith.
And consider 1 Corinthians 7:12–16.
Paul instructs a Christian married to an unbelieving spouse not to initiate separation merely because the spouse does not share the faith, provided the unbelieving spouse is willing to remain.
Marriage and parenthood are different relationships, and that passage cannot be transferred mechanically to every parent-child situation.
But it demonstrates an important principle.
The presence of unbelief in a close family relationship does not automatically make separation a Christian duty.
Then there are Jesus' words in Matthew 10:34–37, where He warns that allegiance to Him may divide households.
These words are serious.
Christ must come before every earthly relationship.
A parent must never deny Jesus to preserve family approval.
A child must never be treated as more authoritative than God.
But Jesus' warning that discipleship may bring division is not permission to manufacture division unnecessarily.
Sometimes faithfulness to Christ will cost you the approval of your family.
That is painful.
But it is very different from deliberately withholding love in order to pressure someone into religious conformity.
Christ calls us to love Him above our families. He does not call us to use our families as targets for spiritual coercion.
There is another passage that deserves attention.
In 2 Timothy 2:24–25, Paul writes:
The Greek phrase ἐν πραΰτητι (en prautēti) means "in gentleness" or "with meekness."
Gentleness is not weakness.
It is strength governed by humility.
And Paul continues by recognizing that repentance is something God may grant.
That should humble every parent who thinks enough arguments, enough pressure, or enough emotional punishment can manufacture genuine conversion.
You can teach.
You can explain.
You can warn.
You can testify.
You can pray.
But you cannot regenerate a human heart.
Jesus told Nicodemus that a person must be born again (John 3:3).
Spiritual rebirth is not something parents can accomplish through control.
Salvation belongs to the Lord.
And perhaps that is the part that hurts most.
Because when your child was small, you could hold their hand while crossing the street.
You could tell them when to sleep.
You could decide which school they attended.
You could bring them to church.
You could teach them Scripture.
But adulthood arrives.
And suddenly you discover that the child whose hand you once held has a conscience, a will, and decisions you cannot control.
You can still influence.
You can still witness.
You can still love.
But you cannot believe on their behalf.
There is a grief in that realization that only a praying parent truly understands.
You can raise a child in a Christian home without being able to guarantee that the child will become a Christian.
Proverbs 22:6 gives wisdom about training a child in the right way. It should not be treated as an unconditional promise that every properly raised child will remain faithful.
The Bible itself contains examples of godly people with unfaithful children and unfaithful parents with godly children.
Every person remains accountable before God.
And that means a child's unbelief is not automatic proof that their parents failed.
Some of you need to hear that.
You have been replaying twenty years of memories, searching for the exact moment you ruined everything.
You wonder whether you should have prayed more.
Been stricter.
Been gentler.
Chosen another church.
Answered that question differently.
Not lost your temper that afternoon.
And while honest self-examination is good, endless self-condemnation is not the same as repentance.
If you sinned, confess it.
If you wounded your child, seek reconciliation.
If you neglected your responsibility, acknowledge it.
But do not appoint yourself the savior of a soul that only Jesus can redeem.
There is only one Christ.
And you are not Him.
Now we must address something equally important.
Does loving an unbelieving adult child mean allowing anything and everything?
Absolutely not.
Christian love does not require parents to surrender their homes to abuse, threats, violence, theft, manipulation, or destructive behavior.
You may need to say:
"I love you, but you cannot threaten people in this house."
"I care about you, but I will not provide money that I know will support destructive behavior."
"You are welcome to talk with me when we can speak respectfully."
"I want a relationship with you, but I cannot continue conversations where you insult or intimidate me."
Those are boundaries.
They are not necessarily rejection.
And in situations involving violence or serious danger, physical separation and professional or legal protection may be necessary.
Forgiveness does not eliminate the need for safety.
Reconciliation does not always mean immediate restoration of trust.
And maintaining love does not mean granting unlimited access to your home, money, or personal life.
Sometimes loving someone requires saying no.
Sometimes it requires allowing an adult child to experience the consequences of their decisions.
Sometimes it means keeping a safe line of communication open while refusing to enable harmful behavior.
But the crucial question is this:
Are you establishing a boundary because something is genuinely harmful, or are you withholding your relationship simply to punish unbelief?
Those motives are not interchangeable.
A boundary protects what is good.
Punishment intended to force faith may produce outward compliance without inward conversion.
And a child who says "I believe" merely to regain parental affection has not necessarily come to saving faith.
God is not glorified by counterfeit repentance.
He desires truth in the inward being, as Psalm 51:6 teaches.
This brings us to another scene in Scripture.
In John 4, Jesus encounters a Samaritan woman at a well.
She belongs to a community marked by deep religious division from the Jews.
Her personal history also becomes part of their conversation.
Jesus does not pretend that theological differences are insignificant.
He tells her plainly that salvation is from the Jews.
He speaks about true worship.
He reveals truth about her life.
Yet He begins by speaking with her.
He treats her as someone worth engaging.
And through that encounter, she becomes a witness to others in her community.
Jesus did not need to compromise truth to cross a social barrier.
He crossed it because truth and grace were not enemies in Him.
John 1:14 describes Jesus as full of grace and truth.
In Greek, χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας (charitos kai alētheias).
Grace and truth.
Not grace without truth.
Not truth without grace.
Both.
And this is where Christian parenting becomes a living testimony.
Your adult child may reject your interpretation of Scripture.
They may reject your church.
They may reject your invitations to worship.
They may even reject the very existence of God.
But when they encounter you, what do they see?
Do they see someone whose love disappears whenever they disagree?
Or someone whose convictions remain firm while their conduct remains marked by patience, humility, and compassion?
Do they see a parent more interested in winning arguments than understanding questions?
Or someone who loves Jesus enough to obey Him even when obedience requires restraint?
You do not have to pretend the distance between your beliefs is small.
Sometimes it is enormous.
But your child should not have to wonder whether you still recognize their humanity.
And now I want to speak to the adult child who may be reading this.
Perhaps you are the one who walked away.
Perhaps your parents sent you this article.
Perhaps you have already decided that Christianity has nothing left to say to you.
I am not asking you to pretend you believe something you do not believe.
And I am not asking you to excuse mistreatment because someone claims to speak for God.
But I want to ask you something.
Have you rejected Jesus Christ Himself, or have you rejected a version of Christianity that was never faithful to His character?
Those are not necessarily the same thing.
Christians can be hypocritical.
Churches can fail.
Parents can sin.
Religious institutions can misuse authority.
None of those failures should be minimized.
But the failures of Christians do not, by themselves, settle the question of whether Jesus is who He claimed to be.
Consider Him.
Read the Gospels.
Examine His words.
Look at His compassion toward the broken, His confrontation of hypocrisy, His call to repentance, His death on the cross, and the testimony of His resurrection.
Do not build your entire conclusion about Christ on the worst behavior of people who claim His name.
And please understand this.
Jesus did not come merely to improve your family's reputation.
He came to save sinners.
That includes religious sinners.
Rebellious sinners.
Self-righteous sinners.
Wounded sinners.
People who have hidden behind church attendance.
And people who have run as far away from church as they possibly could.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." — KJV
The Gospel is not the announcement that good families produce good children.
It is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to a holy God through Jesus Christ.
Christ lived without sin.
He died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
Forgiveness is not earned by having Christian parents.
And it is not received by attending church merely to keep the peace.
It is received through repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.
No family heritage can replace that.
No religious performance can manufacture that.
And no parent's tears can purchase what Christ alone has accomplished.
But His grace is sufficient to save.
And His invitation to repent and believe the Gospel is real.
Now, parent, I want you to imagine something.
It is late at night.
Your phone lights up.
You see your child's name.
The child you have barely spoken to in months.
Perhaps years.
Your heart begins racing.
You answer.
And on the other end, there is silence.
Then a familiar voice whispers:
"Mom?"
Or perhaps:
"Dad?"
And then:
"Can we talk?"
What will that moment find in you?
A speech you have rehearsed for years?
A list of accusations?
A demand for immediate agreement?
Or a heart prepared to listen?
You may not hear the words "I want to come back to Jesus."
Perhaps your child simply needs help.
Perhaps they want to apologize.
Perhaps they want to ask a question.
Perhaps they are lonely.
Perhaps they are still completely unconvinced about Christianity.
And perhaps that phone call is not the moment of conversion you have been praying for.
But it may be a moment when your response can bear witness to the character of Christ.
Do not waste it by trying to control the outcome.
Listen.
Speak truth when appropriate.
Show compassion.
And remember that genuine faith cannot be forced.
There is one more person in Luke 15 we cannot ignore.
The older brother.
While the father rejoiced over the younger son's return, the older brother became angry.
He had remained at home.
He had worked.
He had obeyed.
And now he struggled to celebrate mercy shown to someone who had behaved so disgracefully.
The father came out and pleaded with him too.
What a revealing detail.
The father showed compassion toward the rebellious son.
And patience toward the resentful son.
Jesus told this parable in a setting where religious leaders were complaining that He welcomed sinners.
The story exposes not only rebellion but also self-righteousness.
And that should make every Christian parent examine their heart.
Because sometimes we become so offended by our children's rebellion that we forget how much mercy we ourselves have received.
We begin speaking as though our obedience makes us deserving of God's love.
As though our church attendance has erased our need for grace.
As though the only lost person in the family is the one who stopped attending worship.
But the cross leaves no room for spiritual superiority.
Romans 3:23 says that all have sinned and come short of the glory of God.
The parent needs grace.
The child needs grace.
The preacher needs grace.
The person writing these words needs grace.
And the person reading them needs grace.
Nobody stands at the foot of the cross as a self-made saint.
We stand there as people who need the mercy of Jesus Christ.
So should Christian parents cut off an adult child who rejects their faith?
Not merely because the child no longer believes.
There is no general biblical command requiring parents to sever their relationship with an adult son or daughter simply for rejecting Christianity.
Faithfulness may require difficult boundaries.
It may require refusing to participate in sin.
It may require accepting that your child does not want religious conversations.
It may require distance when a relationship becomes abusive or unsafe.
And in some circumstances, an adult child may choose to end contact despite a parent's willingness to remain connected.
You cannot control that either.
But when a safe and respectful relationship remains possible, Christian parents have strong biblical reasons to pursue love, patience, truthfulness, prayer, and an open door to reconciliation.
Not because unbelief is harmless.
Not because salvation is optional.
Not because every belief leads to God.
But because Jesus Christ is worthy of being represented faithfully.
You are not being asked to surrender the Gospel.
You are being called to live in a manner consistent with it.
And if your child has already been gone for years?
If the messages remain unanswered?
If the holidays have become painful reminders of an empty chair?
If you have prayed until you no longer know what words to use?
Then hear this carefully.
You do not know how your child's story will end.
I cannot promise that every wandering child will return to the faith.
Scripture does not authorize that guarantee.
I cannot promise that every broken family will be reconciled in this lifetime.
And I will not use the pain of a praying parent to manufacture a comforting promise God has not made.
But I can tell you what Scripture does reveal.
God is patient.
God is merciful.
God calls sinners to repentance.
God hears the prayers of His people.
And the Gospel remains the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes (Romans 1:16).
So keep praying.
Not as though prayer gives you control over another person's will.
But because you trust the Lord who is wiser, holier, and more merciful than you.
Keep living faithfully.
Keep examining your own heart.
Keep telling the truth without cruelty.
Keep extending appropriate kindness without surrendering necessary boundaries.
And if a conversation opens, do not treat it as a courtroom where your child must first lose an argument before receiving your love.
Let it be a conversation.
A real one.
Between two human beings who both need grace.
Perhaps tonight, before you sleep, you need to stop rehearsing what your child has done wrong and ask God to search your own heart.
Perhaps you need to send a simple message.
Not a sermon.
Not a warning disguised as a greeting.
Just something honest.
"I know we disagree about faith. I still love you. I would like to hear how you are doing. If I have hurt you, I am willing to listen."
Perhaps you need to apologize.
Perhaps you need to establish a boundary you have been afraid to establish.
Perhaps you need to stop financing destruction.
Perhaps you need to stop confusing your anxiety with the voice of the Holy Spirit.
Or perhaps you need to release the burden of trying to accomplish what only God can do.
Because there is a difference between carrying your child in prayer and trying to carry the weight of your child's salvation.
One is an expression of faith.
The other is a burden no parent was created to bear.
And if this article has reached you while your relationship with your child is breaking apart, I want to ask you something personal.
Have you been trying to protect your faith by closing a door that God never commanded you to close?
Or have you been afraid to establish a necessary boundary because you thought love meant accepting everything?
Be honest before the Lord.
Sometimes repentance begins not with a dramatic public confession but with a quiet recognition that we have allowed fear, anger, or pride to govern our responses.
And sometimes the most Christlike thing a parent can say is:
"Lord, I cannot change my child's heart. But please change whatever is wrong in mine."

And if you are the adult child who has been hurt, confused, or distant, you are welcome in this conversation too. Tell us what you wish Christian parents understood about listening, honesty, and love.
Let this be a place where people speak truthfully, without cruelty.
Because there may be another parent reading the comments at two in the morning, wondering whether anyone else understands the ache of loving a child who no longer shares their faith.
Your words may remind that parent they are not alone.
And if this article brought someone to mind, consider tagging them with sensitivity, especially if doing so will encourage rather than publicly embarrass them.

Better still, send it privately to a mother who has been crying in silence, a father who does not know how to reconnect, or an adult child who needs to know that following Jesus should never be an excuse for cruelty.
Not to expose your family's struggles.
Not to win an argument.
But because there are families quietly breaking apart over questions they have never learned to discuss with both biblical conviction and Christlike compassion.
One thoughtful share may help someone reconsider a painful decision.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, those who have grown cold in their faith, and even those who are not yet Christians to follow along.
Not because we have every answer.
But because the Word of God deserves careful attention, and every human soul deserves to hear the Gospel faithfully proclaimed.
This is also why Gospel Warrior continues creating biblical articles, devotionals, discipleship materials, and resources that address the real struggles people carry behind their smiles.
And I want to speak for a moment to those who have been spiritually nourished by this ministry.
It is a practical way to help sustain and expand this work so that more people can encounter biblical teaching, encouragement, and resources centered on Jesus Christ.
But I want to make something absolutely clear.
Christian giving is to be willing and cheerful, not pressured or manipulated.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that God loves a cheerful giver.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth and opportunities to share the Gospel in everyday life.
But the greater purpose of this ministry will always be spiritual, not commercial.
We want people to open their Bibles.
To understand the Gospel.
To repent of sin.
To receive Christ by faith.
To grow in grace.
To forgive.
To be restored.
To become faithful disciples of Jesus.
The ministry is not the Savior.
Jesus is.
Christ crucified and risen is.
Our calling is to point people toward Him, not to make people dependent upon us.
And that brings us back to the parent sitting alone tonight.
Perhaps the dinner table is set for fewer people than it used to be.
Perhaps your child's old bedroom remains untouched.
Perhaps you still remember the sound of their little voice reciting John 3:16.
Perhaps you wonder whether you will ever hear them pray again.
I cannot tell you when that pain will end.
But I can remind you of something greater than your ability to control the future.
The Lord is still God.
His truth has not changed.
His mercy has not run out.
And your responsibility is not to write the final chapter of another person's soul.
Your responsibility is to remain faithful to Jesus Christ.
To love what He loves.
To reject what He calls sin.
To practice the humility He commands.
To extend the mercy you yourself have received.
To trust Him with what you cannot control.
Because the greatest scandal in the Gospel is not that rebellious children can come home.
It is that a holy God welcomes repentant sinners through the sacrifice of His own Son.
At Calvary, Jesus did not excuse our sin.
He bore its judgment.
He did not pretend we were righteous.
He gave Himself so that sinners could be justified through faith in Him.
He did not offer cheap forgiveness.
He purchased redemption with His blood.
And when He rose from the dead, He proved that sin and death would not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
That is the Gospel.
That is our hope.
That is why we pray.
That is why we speak truth.
That is why we keep loving.
And that is why, when it is safe and right to do so, we leave room for the conversation we thought would never happen.
Not every child will return.
Not every relationship will be restored.
But no parent needs to become cruel to remain faithful.
And no child needs to pretend to believe in order to be treated with human dignity.
So if your son or daughter has walked away from the faith, do not throw away your convictions.
Do not throw away your compassion either.
Hold fast to Christ.
Keep your heart tender.
Let your words be truthful.
Let your boundaries be wise.
Let your prayers be sincere.
And let your life testify that the grace of Jesus Christ is not merely something you preach to strangers.
It is something you are learning to live before the people who know you best.
You may not be able to bring your child back to faith, but you can refuse to let your fear turn your love into another reason they run.
